instructions: Listen to the audio for each part and answer the questions. Each audio plays once.

listeningScripts.title: Gym Membership Cancellation
listeningScripts.text: Member: Hi, I'd like to cancel my gym membership. Customer Service Rep: I'd be happy to help. Can I ask why you're looking to cancel? Member: I'm relocating to British Columbia for work and won't be using the facility anymore. Rep: I understand. Let me pull up your account. What's your membership number? Member: It's GYM-47823. I've been a member for eighteen months. Rep: Great. I see you're on our premium monthly plan at $89 per month. When are you planning to move? Member: Three weeks from now. Rep: Okay. I can process the cancellation effective immediately, or we can set it to end on your move date. Which works better? Member: I prefer the move date, so three weeks from today. Rep: Perfect. That would be June 24th. I'll note that in your file. You won't be charged for July. However, I do need to let you know that you're in the middle of a two-year contract. There is a $150 early termination fee. Member: That's not fair. I wasn't told about that when I signed up. Rep: I apologize for that. Let me see what I can do. Since you've been loyal for eighteen months, I can reduce that fee to $75. That's the best I can offer. Member: Okay, I'll accept that.

listeningScripts.title: Music Concert Plans
listeningScripts.text: Alex: Are you going to the concert next Saturday? Casey: Which one? There are a few shows next weekend. Alex: The indie rock festival at the waterfront. Casey: Oh yeah, I've been thinking about it. How much are tickets? Alex: They're forty dollars each. Casey: That's not too bad. Who's performing? Alex: Five bands. The headliner is The Northern Stars. Casey: Oh, I love them. What time does it start? Alex: Six PM. It should wrap up around eleven. Casey: That's pretty late. Is there parking nearby? Alex: Yeah, there's a parking lot right by the venue. It's five dollars for the whole night. Casey: That's reasonable. Should we get food there or bring our own? Alex: They have food vendors there, but it's probably expensive. Casey: Let's grab something before we go then. Alex: Good idea. Want me to buy your ticket? Casey: Yeah, that would be great. Just send me the bill.

listeningScripts.title: Public Transit New Route Announcement
listeningScripts.text: Good afternoon. Transit Authority is pleased to announce a new rapid bus route effective September 1st. The new Route 95 Express connects downtown to the northern suburbs, with stops at Central Station, City Hall, the Hospital, University Campus, and North Terminal. Service runs Monday through Friday from 6 AM to 10 PM, with departures every fifteen minutes during peak hours, 7 to 9 AM and 4 to 7 PM. Off-peak service is every thirty minutes. Weekend service begins December, with departures every twenty minutes from 9 AM to 8 PM. The Route 95 uses the new dedicated bus lane on Main Street, reducing travel time from downtown to North Terminal from forty-five minutes to approximately twenty-two minutes. Fares are the same as existing routes: single trip is three dollars fifty cents, and a monthly pass is ninety dollars. Seniors and students receive a twenty percent discount. The new buses feature USB charging ports, free Wi-Fi, and comfortable seating. Detailed schedules are available on our website and at all transit stations. Real-time tracking is available through our mobile app.

listeningScripts.title: New Brunswick Fisheries Management Plan
listeningScripts.text: New Brunswick has introduced a comprehensive fisheries management plan aimed at rebuilding declining fish stocks and supporting the province's fishing communities. The plan allocates 67 million dollars over five years to research, enforcement, and sustainable fishing initiatives. Atlantic salmon populations have declined by 48 percent over the past two decades, prompting urgent action. The plan imposes stricter catch limits on cod and halibut in designated zones. Fishing vessel owners participating in conservation programs receive subsidies up to 200,000 dollars for upgrading to eco-friendly equipment. The program mandates trap modifications to reduce unintended marine mammal bycatch by 35 percent. Over 3,200 fishermen and their families depend on this industry in New Brunswick. The province is establishing a new fisheries research center employing 120 marine scientists. Marine Protected Areas will expand to cover an additional 8 percent of provincial waters. The plan aims to achieve sustainable fish stock levels by 2032.

listeningScripts.title: Workplace Safety Initiative
listeningScripts.text:
Safety Officer Tom: I've been analyzing our workplace incident reports from the past two years, and I'm concerned about our trend. We've had 34 reported injuries this year, which is up 15 percent from last year. Most incidents are slips, trips, and falls in warehouse areas. I'm proposing we implement mandatory safety training for all warehouse staff every six months, not annually as we currently do.

Warehouse Manager David: Tom, I appreciate your concern, but I'm worried about requiring training every six months. That's a lot of time away from work. My team's productivity is already under pressure with current targets. If we pull people off the floor for training frequently, we'll fall further behind on our goals. Can't we just focus on better signage and equipment?

Worker Representative Angela: I actually support Tom's proposal. I work in the warehouse, and I've seen some close calls that could have been serious. The issue isn't signage—we know the hazards. The problem is we get complacent. Regular training keeps safety top of mind. Plus, Tom, I think twice-yearly training would actually improve morale because workers feel the company cares about their wellbeing.

Safety Officer Tom: Thank you, Angela. David, I understand your concern about productivity, but consider the cost of injuries. Each workplace injury costs us about $12,000 in direct and indirect costs. If we can prevent even three injuries per year, the training pays for itself. And research shows regular safety training actually reduces injuries, which ultimately improves productivity.

listeningScripts.title: Mental Health Parity in Insurance Coverage
listeningScripts.text: Mental health needs to be treated with the same importance as physical health in our insurance system. We talk about mental health awareness, but when it comes to actual coverage, it's dramatically underfunded. Most insurance plans cover mental health at lower rates than physical health. If you have a broken arm, insurance covers months of physical therapy. If you have depression or anxiety, you get maybe 10 sessions of therapy a year, and psychologist visits might only be 50 percent covered. This creates barriers. Many people avoid treatment because they can't afford it, and their conditions worsen. The economic impact is massive. Mental health issues cost the economy 51 billion dollars annually in Canada through lost productivity, emergency services, and hospitalizations. Yet we invest a fraction of that in prevention and treatment. Here's what frustrates me most: we have effective treatments. Therapy works. Medication helps. But access is limited by insurance coverage. A person struggling with bipolar disorder shouldn't have to choose between therapy and rent. Insurance companies argue coverage limits are necessary for cost control, but that's shortsighted. When people get mental health treatment early, they use fewer emergency services, work more, and contribute to society. The ROI on mental health coverage is actually positive. I'm advocating for mandatory parity—insurance companies should cover mental health at the same level as physical health. This means removing visit limits, lowering copayments, and covering evidence-based treatments. It's not just compassionate; it's economically smart.
